milestones.title: A workspace, a boot, and options of your own
milestones.body:
First get Zephyr itself working: follow **One-time setup** in the starter's `README.md` (the Workshop lesson walks through the same steps) until the `hello_world` smoke test runs. It takes a while, mostly downloading, and that's fine. If it stops, the README's **Stuck at setup?** table goes through the usual causes in order.

Then make the skeleton yours:

```
$ make run
[00:00:00.000,000] <inf> sensor_node: sensor node starting on native_sim
[00:00:00.000,000] <inf> sensor_node: sampling every 100 ms, reporting every 1000 ms
```

**Three Kconfig options**, in the app's `Kconfig`, inside the `Sensor node` menu, each an `int` with a prompt, a range and a help text:

| Option | Default | Allowed |
|---|---|---|
| `SENSOR_NODE_SAMPLE_MS` | 100 | 10 to 10000 |
| `SENSOR_NODE_REPORT_MS` | 1000 | 10 to 60000 |
| `SENSOR_NODE_QUEUE_LEN` | 8 | 1 to 64 |

`main` logs the two periods from them at startup, as above. Then experiment: open `west build -d build/app -t menuconfig`, find your menu, and press `?` on an option. Set `CONFIG_SENSOR_NODE_SAMPLE_MS=250` in `prj.conf` and check that the log follows. Then try a value outside the range and read what the build says.

**Done when** `make run` prints both lines and `make test-m1` is green.
hints: Where does a CONFIG_ symbol come from before it reaches your C code? Which file declares it, which file sets it, and which generated header finally defines it?

Kconfig and prj.conf are in west, Kconfig & the build, and the Workshop lesson adds an option of its own and reads the out-of-range error. An option's type, prompt, default, range and help are all lines under its config entry, and the app's Kconfig already has the menu and the line that pulls in the rest of Zephyr. If the build stops on the setup, work down the README's Stuck at setup? table: venv, west, ZEPHYR_BASE, CMake, hello_world, then a clean build.

Finish the setup and get hello_world running first. Then add the three config entries inside the menu, above the line that sources Kconfig.zephyr, and log the two periods in main using their CONFIG_ names. Rebuild, run, and look in build/app/zephyr/.config to see the values Kconfig settled on.

milestones.title: A sensor in the devicetree
milestones.body:
There's no real sensor, so you'll write a driver for a pretend one. Its binding is given: `dts/bindings/vnd,ramp-temp.yaml` describes a temperature sensor whose samples walk up a ramp (`start`, `start + step`, ...) for `ramp-steps` values and then start over.

**The driver** is a real Zephyr sensor driver. `src/ramp_temp.c` has the plumbing (the compatible, the config filled from the devicetree, the API struct and the macro that creates one device per node, as in Writing a Zephyr driver) and empty functions with TODOs. The behaviour is yours:

- One device instance for **every** enabled `vnd,ramp-temp` node, each with its own ramp. A fresh instance's first sample is `start-millicelsius`.
- Fetching `SENSOR_CHAN_ALL` or `SENSOR_CHAN_AMBIENT_TEMP` takes the next value of the ramp. Any other channel returns `-ENOTSUP`.
- Getting `SENSOR_CHAN_AMBIENT_TEMP` returns the last fetched value as a `struct sensor_value`: whole degrees in `val1`, millionths in `val2` (21.250 °C is `val1 = 21`, `val2 = 250000`). Any other channel returns `-ENOTSUP`.
- A node with `ramp-steps` below 1 makes `device_is_ready()` false instead of crashing later.

**The node**: add one to `app.overlay` with the alias `ambient-temp`, and pick the ramp you like. The rest of the app will find the sensor through that alias only.

The tests read sensors from their own `tests/app.overlay` through the standard sensor API, so they don't care how you name things inside the driver.

**Done when** `make test-m2` is green and `make build` builds with your overlay.
hints: Two nodes with the same compatible must give two independent sensors. The skeleton already gives each one its own config; what else has to be per instance, and how does fetch find it from the device pointer it's handed?

Writing a Zephyr driver is this milestone in miniature: config is read-only and comes from the devicetree, data is the instance's mutable state, and both reach your functions through dev->config and dev->data. struct sensor_value is whole units in val1 and millionths in val2, and sensor_value_from_milli does the conversion. Devicetree & bindings explains the undefined __device_dts_ord link error if a node has no driver. The sensor subsystem also needs CONFIG_SENSOR in prj.conf.

Put the position on the ramp and the last sample in the data struct. In fetch, reject other channels with -ENOTSUP, compute start plus position times step, then advance the position and wrap it at ramp-steps. In get, reject other channels and convert the last sample. In init, return -EINVAL when ramp-steps is below 1. Then add a node and the ambient-temp alias to app.overlay, and build once more with make clean if the overlay is new.

milestones.title: Sample, queue, process
milestones.body:
Now make the node do its job, in two threads:

- **Sampling** reads `ambient-temp` every `SENSOR_NODE_SAMPLE_MS`, steadily: a slow reading mustn't push every later sample back.
- Each sample goes to a **processing** thread through a message queue that holds `SENSOR_NODE_QUEUE_LEN` samples. Sampling never waits for room: if the queue is full, the sample is dropped and counted.
- Processing keeps **statistics since the last reset**: the number of samples, min, max and mean (the mean of the millidegrees, truncated).
- Both threads start on their own when the system boots. `main` doesn't start them, and the tests don't have your `main`.

**The shell**: enable it and add a `node` command with two subcommands.

```
uart:~$ node stats
samples=10 min=20.000 max=21.500 mean=20.750 dropped=0
uart:~$ node reset
uart:~$ node stats
samples=0 min=n/a max=n/a mean=n/a dropped=0
```

Temperatures always have exactly three decimals. With no samples, `min`, `max` and `mean` are `n/a`. `node reset` clears everything `node stats` shows.

Why `node` and not `sensor`? `sensor` is the name of Zephyr's own sensor shell. It's off by default, but the day someone turns on `CONFIG_SENSOR_SHELL` to debug a driver, two commands would share a name.

**Done when** `make test-m3` is green, and in `make run` the numbers in `node stats` keep growing.
hints: Three parties now touch the statistics: processing writes them, the shell reads and clears them, and soon a report will read them. What could a reader see if it caught the writer halfway through one update?

Message queues covers K_MSGQ_DEFINE and why the producer calls k_msgq_put with K_NO_WAIT and counts drops. k_sem & k_mutex covers K_MUTEX_DEFINE for the shared data, and Threads: cooperative vs preemptive covers K_THREAD_DEFINE and priorities (lower number is more urgent; keep these preemptible). For a steady period, sleep with k_sleep until an absolute K_TIMEOUT_ABS_MS deadline rather than k_msleep. The shell command is a SHELL_STATIC_SUBCMD_SET_CREATE list of SHELL_CMD entries, registered with SHELL_CMD_REGISTER, printing with shell_print (the README's APIs table links the docs).

Keep the statistics in one module that owns a mutex and offers add, count a drop, reset and copy everything out. Define the queue with the Kconfig length, a sampler thread that reads, puts without waiting and sleeps until its next deadline, and a processing thread that blocks on k_msgq_get with K_FOREVER and adds each sample. In the shell module, stats copies the statistics out, formats them and prints one line, and reset clears them. Write one helper that turns millidegrees into text with three decimals and use it everywhere.

milestones.title: A report every period
milestones.body:
Every `SENSOR_NODE_REPORT_MS` the node logs a **report** at info level with the number of samples, min, max, mean and dropped since the last reset. The wording is yours:

```
[00:00:05.000,000] <inf> reporter: report: 50 samples, min 21.000, max 22.750, mean 21.875 C, 0 dropped
```

- The timing comes from a **periodic kernel timer**, started once. Nothing reads the timer in a loop, and nothing restarts it every time.
- The statistics are never touched from interrupt context.
- A report doesn't reset the statistics.
- The numbers in one report come from **the same moment**: the sample count and the sum that make the mean are never from two different points in time.
- `node stats` ends with `reports=N`, the number of reports since the last reset. `node reset` sets it back to 0.

**Done when** `make test-m4` is green and `make run` logs a report every second.
hints: Which context does a k_timer's expiry callback run in, and what are you allowed to do there? If the answer rules out what the report needs, who could do the report instead?

k_timer & periodic work is exactly this pattern: the K_TIMER_DEFINE expiry callback only calls k_work_submit on a K_WORK_DEFINE item, and the work runs later in the system workqueue thread, where taking a mutex and logging with LOG_INF are fine (Workqueues: deferring ISR work). The test image has CONFIG_ASSERT on, so a mutex in the expiry stops the run with an assertion. The sensor hub boss explains copying the statistics under the lock and formatting the copy after unlocking.

Define a work item whose handler counts the report, copies the statistics in one locked step and logs the copy (its own LOG_MODULE_REGISTER gives the reporter: prefix). Define a timer whose expiry does nothing but submit that work. Start it once with k_timer_start, the report period as both the first delay and the period, from a SYS_INIT hook at the APPLICATION level: it runs before main and works in the test image too. Add the report count to the statistics so stats prints it and reset clears it.

milestones.title: Operator controls
milestones.body:
Two more subcommands for whoever is on the console:

**`node read`** reads the sensor right now and prints it:

```
uart:~$ node read
ambient: 21.250 C
```

It must be safe while sampling is running: a reading from the shell must never get the value of someone else's fetch.

**`node period <ms>`** changes the report period, taking effect immediately. The value is a whole number of milliseconds from 10 to 60000. Anything else is rejected with an error message on the shell's error output, a non-zero return value and the period left unchanged. That includes a missing value, `abc`, `200x`, `-100`, `5` and `70000`.

```
uart:~$ node period 250
report period 250 ms
uart:~$ node period 5
period must be a whole number of ms from 10 to 60000
```

**Done when** `make test-m5` is green, and the whole `make test` (or `make twister`) passes.
hints: Reading a sensor is two calls, a fetch and a get. What happens if the sampler's fetch lands between the shell's fetch and its get? And for the period: which inputs would a quick conversion with no error checking turn into a number that looks valid?

Serialising a two-step operation on a shared device is the mutex use from k_sem & k_mutex: the lock covers the sensor_sample_fetch and sensor_channel_get pair, not each call. Calling k_timer_start again on a running timer is allowed and takes effect at once (k_timer & periodic work). SHELL_CMD_ARG declares how many arguments a subcommand needs, so the shell rejects a missing one for you; a handler reports failure with shell_error and a negative errno such as -EINVAL.

Put the fetch and get pair behind one lock in one helper that both the sampler and the shell use. For read, call it and print the value with the three-decimal helper. For period, convert the text with strtol and its end pointer, reject it unless the end pointer moved and landed on the end of the string and the number is in range, and only then restart the timer and confirm with shell_print.
